data.body: Websites changed. Most platforms didn't.

WordPress changed how the world built websites, and it deserves that legacy. But the internet it was created for in 2003 is not the internet we build for today.

Websites are now applications. They talk to payment systems, CRMs and internal tools. They serve logged-in customers, not just readers. Performance is measured in milliseconds, security is a board-level concern, and development teams work with frameworks, APIs and version control, not FTP.

Most established platforms have spent twenty years adapting to that shift. Magna CMS was designed inside it.

data.body: Answers to common questions

items.question: What is Magna CMS?
items.answer: Magna CMS is an open-source, extensible content management system built on a contemporary framework. It pairs visual tools for content teams with a plugin architecture designed for developers. It's a foundation for websites and the applications they grow into.

items.question: Is Magna headless?
items.answer: Magna is headless-first: content is served over an API, so any frontend can consume it: a JavaScript framework, a mobile app, multiple channels at once. But headless is a choice, not a constraint: switch on the ready-made website frontend with one click when you just want a site, and move between the two approaches without re-platforming.

items.question: Is Magna trying to replace WordPress?
items.answer: No. WordPress shaped the web and remains a strong choice for many projects. Magna takes a different approach: it was designed in this decade, around today's architecture, security expectations and workflows. The right platform depends on the project.

items.question: Who is Magna for?
items.answer: Developers who want a CMS that behaves like the software they already build, agencies standardising on a reusable stack, businesses whose projects may outgrow "website", and content teams who want to publish without a developer on call.

items.question: Can I build my own plugins?
items.answer: Yes. That's the point of the architecture. Plugins are the supported way to add functionality, with first-class extension points. Custom development is a normal path, not a workaround, and your code stays upgrade-safe and version-controlled.

data.body: Build your next project on a foundation from this decade
Whether it starts as a website or a platform, Magna gives you a core worth building on: open, extensible and designed for the web you're building now.
The web hasn't stopped evolving. Neither should the platform underneath it.
Magna CMS exists because of a simple observation: the tools most of the web runs on were designed for a different web. This page explains what we're building, and why.
Two decades is a long time in software

The first great CMS platforms, WordPress chief among them, solved a real problem brilliantly. They put publishing in the hands of everyone, and in doing so they shaped the modern web. That contribution deserves respect, not revisionism.

But longevity has a cost. Decades of evolution also mean decades of accumulated technical decisions, backwards compatibility obligations and layered complexity. Every early choice, sensible at the time, becomes something later versions must carry.

None of this makes older platforms bad. It makes them products of their era. The question worth asking is different:

data.quote: If we were designing a CMS today, for today's websites, teams and threats, what would we choose? Magna CMS is our answer.

The core does content management thoroughly and dependably, and resists scope creep. A smaller, well-understood core is easier to secure, maintain and trust.

Magna doesn't assume you're building a blog, a shop or anything else. Whatever the project becomes, the platform doesn't stand in the way.
Judge it by what it lets you build
Philosophy is cheap. Open the features, read the code, build something on it.

data.body: Your solution could be someone's missing piece
Developers and agencies can build plugins for their own projects, or package and share them. As the ecosystem grows, the expertise you encode becomes distribution.
A platform should grow the way your project does: piece by deliberate piece.
Keep the core focused. Add what you need.
Start with content. Extend when the project asks for it.
It started with a question
If we were building a CMS today, knowing everything the last twenty years taught us, what would it look like? Magna CMS is the working answer.
The web grew up. We kept noticing.

We've spent years building for the web, as developers and alongside the agencies and businesses that live on it. Over that time, a pattern kept repeating.

The web changed profoundly. Sites became applications. Content became a system. Security became existential. Development matured into a proper engineering discipline, with frameworks, APIs and workflows that would be unrecognisable to 2003.

And yet, so often, projects still began on platforms designed before any of that: brilliant for their time, endlessly patched since, carrying every era of their own history. We watched talented teams spend their best hours working around their tools instead of with them.

The platforms weren't wrong. They were simply from another time. That distinction matters, and it pointed at the question we couldn't put down: what would this look like if it were designed now?
A foundation, not just another CMS
Magna is our answer, built on convictions the last two decades earned.

data.body: Early, ambitious, and building in the open

Magna is young, and we say that plainly. The core is real, the architecture is the point, and the ecosystem is growing into it. What we're building towards is a platform where the question is never "can the CMS do this?" but only "what should we build next?"
If that's the kind of foundation you want under your work, we'd like you building on it, or with us.
Build with us, or on us
Open code, open roadmap, honest labels. That's the whole pitch.
A different approach to content management

Established platforms like WordPress shaped the web, and they remain the right choice for many projects. Magna takes a different path, designed in this decade around today's requirements. Here's the philosophical difference, stated plainly.

Platforms inherit the assumptions of their era. A CMS designed in the early 2000s optimised for publishing pages to readers. A CMS designed now assumes websites are applications, teams work like engineering organisations, and requirements change mid-flight.

Neither assumption set is wrong. They're answers to different questions.
Two eras, two sets of assumptions

data.rows:
Area | Traditional CMS approach | Magna CMS approach
Architecture | Foundations from an earlier era, evolved carefully over decades | Laravel-native architecture designed today
Delivery | Server-rendered pages first; headless as a bolt-on | Headless-first API, with a website frontend you can switch on
Content schema | Generic post tables with layered metadata | Schema as code, synced to real, typed database tables
Core scope | Feature-rich cores grown by accretion | Deliberately focused core; everything else modular
Extensibility | Vast ecosystems of varying quality, compatibility and security | Composer packages with manifests, declared permissions and a fault-tolerant runtime
Security | Hardened over time, often via plugins | Argon2id, 2FA, scoped API keys, RBAC and an append-only audit log as defaults
Development | Workflows shaped by platform history | Version control, environments and framework conventions as the default path
Applications | Primarily website-focused; applications possible with effort | Designed for websites and the applications they become

data.body: Own your platform, own your data

Hosted headless platforms are excellent products, but you pay per record, per call and per seat, on infrastructure you'll never own. Magna is MIT-licensed and self-hosted: no per-record fees, no seat limits, no vendor lock-in.

data.body: The right platform depends on the project

If you need the largest possible theme catalogue, a plugin for almost anything, and two decades of community answers, then a mature platform like WordPress remains a strong, sensible choice. We won't pretend otherwise. Magna is designed for a different profile of team:
